title: 机器学习中的训练集、验证集与测试集：如何划分数据而不造成数据泄漏
author: otwosoft
content:
Every machine learning project starts with data, but the way you divide that data decides whether your results mean anything. A model that scores 98 percent in training may fail badly on new examples. This guide explains what each split does, how to choose split ratios, where leakage creeps in, and how to use cross-validation when data is scarce.

What is a train, validation, and test split?

A train, validation, and test split divides one dataset into three separate subsets, and each subset has a different job. The training set fits the model parameters, the validation set tunes choices such as hyperparameters, and the test set gives one final unbiased score on examples the model has never seen. Keeping the three jobs separate is what makes the final score trustworthy.

The training set is the largest part of the data and the only part the model learns from directly. During training, the algorithm adjusts its internal parameters to reduce error on these examples. The validation set is never used to fit parameters. Instead, it is used to compare choices: which value of k works best in k-nearest neighbors, how deep a tree should grow, or when to stop training before the model starts memorizing noise. The test set stays untouched until the very end, when the final model is scored on it once for an honest estimate of performance on new data.

This three-way division is the foundation of honest evaluation in supervised learning. A clear explanation of training, validation, and test data shows how the three subsets work together: training fits, validation tunes, and testing measures. If you are still building your mental model of the field, a plain overview of what is machine learning is a useful starting point.

Why do you need three splits instead of two?

Two splits are not enough, because tuning on the test set quietly turns it into a second validation set and destroys the unbiased final score. Every time you adjust a model based on test results, the test set stops being unseen data and starts being part of the training process. Three splits exist to prevent exactly that.

You train a model and check it on the validation set. The score tells you the model is underfitting, so you increase its capacity and check again. Each tuning choice is guided by the validation set. By the end of this process, the model has been shaped by the validation set, even though it never trained on it directly. The validation score is therefore optimistic, because it reflects a model tuned to do well on that particular set of examples.

The test set is the only protection against that optimism, and it works only if it stays untouched until tuning is finished. The moment you use test results to change a hyperparameter or pick between two candidate models, the test set has become another validation set, and you no longer have an unbiased estimate of real-world performance. The rule is simple and strict: the test set is opened once, at the end, for a single final measurement.

The third split also matters for detecting overfitting. A model that memorizes its training data will show a large gap between training accuracy and validation accuracy, and that gap signals overfitting. Understanding overfitting in machine learning helps you read that gap correctly: a small gap with low scores on both sets points to underfitting, while a large gap with a high training score points to memorization rather than learning.

What goes wrong when the test set leaks?

Leakage means information from the test set influences training or tuning, so the test score looks better than the model really is. The model appears accurate in evaluation and then underperforms on genuinely new data, because the evaluation was never honest in the first place.

The most common form of leakage is preprocessing the full dataset before splitting it. If you compute a scaler, an imputer, or a text vectorizer on all the data and then split, the training set has already seen statistics from the test set. The correct order is to split first and fit every preprocessing step on the training set only, then apply the same fitted transformation to the validation and test sets. The same applies to feature selection on the whole dataset, which also inflates the final score.

Duplicate rows are another quiet source of leakage. Near-duplicates mean a random split can place one copy in the training set and another in the test set. The model then appears to generalize when it is really recognizing examples it has seen. Deduplication before splitting, or grouping related rows so that all copies land in the same subset, prevents this.

Time-ordered data leaks differently. If your data has a time dimension, such as sales records or sensor readings, a random split mixes past and future. The model can then learn from future examples to predict past ones, which cannot happen in production. Time-based data needs a chronological split: earlier data for training, later data for validation, and the latest data for testing.

How do you choose split ratios like 80/10/10?

Common ratios are 80/10/10 or 70/15/15, and the right choice depends on dataset size, the number of classes, and how much tuning you plan to do. There is no single ratio that fits every project, but the trade-offs are straightforward.

The training set needs to be large enough for the model to learn the pattern. With a small dataset, a 60/20/20 split may leave too little training data, and the model underperforms for lack of examples. With a large dataset, an 80/10/10 split still leaves plenty of examples for validation and testing while giving the model most of the data to learn from. As a rule of thumb, the training share grows with dataset size, while the validation and test shares can shrink in percentage terms.

The validation set needs to be large enough to distinguish between candidate models. If you are comparing ten hyperparameter settings and the validation set has only fifty examples, the differences between settings will be noise. The test set needs the same: enough examples for a meaningful final score. A test set of twenty examples cannot support a serious claim about accuracy, because a single example changes the score by five percentage points.

Class balance changes the calculation. When one class is rare, a random split can leave the validation or test set with almost no examples of that class. Stratified splitting fixes this by preserving the class proportions in every subset, so each split contains a representative mix. Stratification should be the default whenever the target is a category rather than a number.

What is cross-validation and when should you use it?

Cross-validation rotates the validation role across folds so that every example is used for both training and validation, which gives a more stable estimate when data is scarce. Instead of relying on a single validation split, you divide the data into k folds, train on k minus one folds, validate on the remaining fold, and repeat until each fold has served as the validation set once. The average of the k scores is more reliable than any single split.

The most common form is k-fold cross-validation with k set to five or ten. Five folds is a good balance between stability and compute cost, since it requires training five models instead of one. Ten folds is slightly more stable at twice the cost. Stratified k-fold preserves class proportions in each fold and is the right default for classification problems. For time-ordered data, each validation fold must come after its training folds in time.

Cross-validation is most valuable when the dataset is small. With only a few hundred examples, a single validation split may be unrepresentative, and the ranking of candidate models can flip depending on which examples happen to land in the validation set. It is also the standard way to tune hyperparameters, since the average across folds is a fairer basis for comparing settings.

Cross-validation does not replace the test set. The folds are used for tuning, which means the cross-validated score is still an optimistic estimate, just a less noisy one. The honest final measurement still comes from a held-out test set that was never used in any fold. The scikit-learn documentation on cross-validation describes the standard patterns, including k-fold, stratified, and time series splits, and it is a solid reference for the exact behavior of each variant.

How do you split data for different kinds of models?

The split strategy changes with the task, because different kinds of models face different risks. A single random split is fine for some problems and misleading for others, so the choice should follow the structure of the data.

For ordinary supervised learning on tabular data, a random or stratified split is usually correct, provided the examples are independent of each other. Well-known benchmarks such as MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet ship with fixed splits so that results from different teams can be compared fairly. When you use a benchmark, keep its official split instead of inventing your own, because changing it makes your numbers incomparable with published results.

For time series and other ordered data, the split must be chronological. Random shuffling would let the model peek at the future, so the training period comes first, the validation period second, and the test period last. For grouped data, such as multiple records from the same patient, customer, or device, the split must keep each group whole. Splitting by group ensures the model is tested on groups it has never seen, which honestly measures generalization to new groups.

For clustering and unsupervised learning there is no labeled target to stratify on, but splits are still useful: fitting a clustering on one subset and checking its stability on another tells you whether the clusters are real structure or an artifact of one particular sample. For large language model fine-tuning, a held-out set of prompts and expected outputs, kept separate from the fine-tuning data, is the only way to tell whether the tuned model improved or simply memorized its training prompts.

What are the most common splitting mistakes?

The most common splitting mistakes are preprocessing before splitting, tuning on the test set, using random splits for time-ordered data, ignoring class balance, and reusing the test set after peeking at its results. Each of these is easy to make and easy to prevent once you know to look for it.

Preprocessing before splitting is the mistake that appears most often in tutorials and starter code, because fitting a scaler on the full dataset is one line of code and looks harmless. The fix is mechanical: split first, fit preprocessing on the training set only, and apply the fitted transformer to the other sets. Any step that learns something from the data must learn it from the training set alone.

Tuning on the test set is the mistake that costs the most credibility, because it invalidates the only unbiased measurement you have. The fix is procedural: decide in advance that the test set is opened once, at the end. If the test score disappoints, the honest response is to improve the model and re-tune on the validation set, not to adjust the model until the test score looks good.

Chronological splits fix ordered data, and stratified splits fix class balance. But reusing a test set across many experiments slowly turns it into a validation set, because each experiment leaks a little information about it. When a test set has guided many decisions, the right move is to collect a fresh held-out set or accept that the reported score is optimistic.

Conclusion

Train, validation, and test splits are a simple idea with strict rules, and those rules are what make model evaluation honest. The training set fits the model, the validation set guides tuning, and the test set gives one final unbiased score. Leakage breaks the separation at any of these steps. Sensible ratios, stratification, chronological splits, and cross-validation keep the evaluation trustworthy. A model evaluated this way may score lower than a leaky one, but its score means something, and that is the whole point of the split.

FAQs

Can I use the test set more than once?

No, not if you want the score to stay unbiased. Opening the test set once for a final measurement is the rule. Every additional use turns it further into a validation set. If you need to evaluate again after changing the model, re-tune on the validation set instead.

How big should the validation set be?

It should be large enough to rank candidate models reliably. For most projects, 10 to 20 percent of the data is a reasonable validation share. If the validation scores of competing models differ by less than the noise in the measurement, the validation set is too small to decide between them.

Is cross-validation a replacement for a test set?

No. Cross-validation improves the tuning process by averaging across folds, but the folds are still used to make decisions, so the cross-validated score is optimistic. A held-out test set that never took part in any fold is still needed for the final unbiased measurement.

What should I do if my dataset is very small?

Use cross-validation for tuning so that every example contributes to both training and validation, and keep a small held-out test set for the final check even if it is only a few dozen examples. With very small data, the test score will be noisy, so report it alongside the cross-validated scores.
aiSummary: 本指南全面阐述了正确划分机器学习训练集、验证集和测试集的重要性，说明如何防止数据泄漏并确保模型评估结果可靠。
oneSentenceSummary: 本指南全面阐述了正确划分机器学习训练集、验证集和测试集的重要性，说明如何防止数据泄漏并确保模型评估结果可靠。
summary: 本文深入讲解了机器学习中的训练集、验证集和测试集，强调三者各自的作用，以及数据划分不当会造成的后果。每个数据集都有特定用途：训练集用于拟合模型参数，验证集用于调整超参数，测试集则用于提供无偏的最终评分。文章还探讨了常见问题，包括划分数据前进行预处理、测试集泄漏、对有时间顺序的数据进行随机划分，以及类别不平衡。指南就如何选择划分比例、采用分层划分和按时间顺序划分，以及如何在小型数据集中实施交叉验证，提供了实用建议。文章最后强调，严格遵守这些数据隔离规则，才能诚实地评估模型，即使评估分数低于存在数据泄漏时的结果。

mainPoints.point: 三种不同的数据集划分在模型评估中各有用途
mainPoints.explanation: 训练集用于拟合模型参数，验证集用于调整超参数和选择模型，测试集则用于提供一次无偏的最终评分。要确保评估结果可靠，就必须将这三种用途严格区分。

mainPoints.point: 数据泄漏会使模型评估失去效力
mainPoints.explanation: 如果测试集中的信息影响了训练或调参，测试分数就会过于乐观。常见的数据泄漏来源包括划分数据前进行预处理、存在重复行，以及不当处理有时间顺序或分组的数据。

mainPoints.point: 小型数据集需要使用交叉验证
mainPoints.explanation: 通过在不同折中轮流使用验证集，交叉验证能在数据稀少时提供更稳定的估计。不过，它不能取代留出的测试集；最终仍需使用测试集进行无偏测量。

mainPoints.point: 划分策略必须适应数据特征
mainPoints.explanation: 独立的表格数据适合随机划分，有时间顺序的数据必须按时间顺序划分；如果多条记录属于同一实体（如患者、客户或设备），则应采用分组划分以防止数据泄漏。

keyQuotes: 「每个机器学习项目都始于数据，但如何划分数据，决定了最终结果是否有意义。」
「测试集是防止这种过度乐观的唯一保障；只有在调参结束前始终不触碰它，这种保障才有效。」
「规则简单而严格：测试集只在最后打开一次，用于进行一次最终测量。」
「训练集、验证集和测试集的划分看似简单，却有严格规则；正是这些规则，才能让模型评估保持诚实。」
